author.bio: Simone de Beauvoir was a French existentialist philosopher, novelist and essayist, and a central figure of 20th-century feminist thought. Her 1949 study Le Deuxième Sexe (The Second Sex) argued that “woman” is a social construction rather than a biological destiny, a thesis compressed into its most quoted sentence. She won the Prix Goncourt in 1954 for her novel Les Mandarins.

misattribution.heading: The words are Beauvoir’s — but the English is a translator’s
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Beauvoir is correct. The subtlety worth knowing is that Beauvoir wrote in French, and the celebrated English sentence is a translation whose exact wording has changed over time.

items.why: Beauvoir wrote “On ne naît pas femme : on le devient” in 1949. The familiar English “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman” is H. M. Parshley’s 1953 rendering, not Beauvoir’s own English.

The 2009 complete translation deliberately drops the article — “One is not born, but rather becomes, woman” — to signal that Beauvoir means woman as a constructed category, per the discussion of the two translations.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the French are genuinely Beauvoir’s, opening Volume II of The Second Sex (1949); the exact English line quoted everywhere is Parshley’s 1953 translation.

context.heading: Why the line mattered
lead: Opening the volume on women’s “lived experience,” the sentence distilled Beauvoir’s central claim: that femininity is produced by culture and situation, not fixed by biology. It became a founding statement for later distinctions between biological sex and socially constructed gender.
Because it is so compressed, the line travels well — and often travels detached from its source, which is why its status as a 1953 translation of a 1949 French text is so frequently lost.
